chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter takes place at Lali's craft table. Paper cutouts, a windmill firki, wooden printing blocks and cards of letters and digits show what a line of symmetry is, what it means for a shape to look the same after a turn, and how to tell the two apart. A short video explains each idea, and an interactive tool lets the student try it alone.

points.title: Videos teach, tools explore
points.text: Every idea has one short concept video. The tool that follows is where the student explores, builds and checks the idea alone, with hints, retry and reset. Four tools, each with its own purpose, follow the chapter's own plan.

points.title: A tool in three steps
points.text: Each tool opens with a short recall of the video idea, then lets the student play and apply it, and ends with the chapter's own question, used exactly as the book gives it.

points.title: Every book question has its own video
points.text: Every solved example, Let Us Do question and every answerable prompt of the book is its own short video with a step by step solution and a question picture and a solution picture, in a Questions topic that follows the idea it practises.

points.title: Two tests for symmetry
points.text: A fold line tests reflection symmetry and a turn tests rotational symmetry. A shape can pass one, both or neither, so the student runs both tests every time.

points.title: Only the book's shapes
points.text: Letters, digits, designs and block prints are the book's own. Any shape or number the plan adds is a practice value and is said to be one.

media.title: Fold and Cut

tool_config.title: Fold and Cut
tool_config.idea: Find out by folding and cutting that a letter with a line of symmetry can be made by drawing only half of it (one fold) or a quarter of it (two folds), and that a fold on a line that is not a line of symmetry gives a cutout that is not the letter. This is the free first try of the chapter, so it asks and shows; the video that follows names the idea.
tool_config.screen: Lali's craft table, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation, with the Happy Birthday wall banner behind it. A large square sheet of coloured paper lies in the middle of the table and is the largest thing on screen, with a dashed vertical fold line and a dashed horizontal fold line marked on it. On the left a shelf holds letter cards, each card a plain capital letter. A pair of scissors and a pencil lie beside the paper. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: tap a letter card to put its outline on the paper; three fold buttons, Vertical, Horizontal and Both ways (one-fourth); a Draw button that shows the part of the letter to draw along the fold; a Cut button that cuts along the outline; an Open button that unfolds the paper and shows the cutout; a results sheet on the right with a row for each letter and three columns, horizontal line, vertical line and both, that the student ticks; Check, Hint, Retry (unfolds the paper for this card), Reset (clears the results sheet), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the fold chosen, the part drawn (1/2 or 1/4), a message under the opened paper saying whether the cutout is the full letter, and a card number out of 7.
student_does: Look at the folded paper from the story, with half of the letter A drawn along the fold. Tap the line on the paper where it is folded, then press Next.
Choose a letter, choose a fold, press Draw, Cut and Open, and see whether the cutout is the full letter. Cut A with one fold, H with two folds, M and B with the right fold, and try F with every fold.

Answer the questions from the story: which of the letters E, N, X, T, K, V and O can be made by just drawing half or a quarter, and which have a horizontal line, a vertical line or both. Cut each letter and tick the results sheet.
challenges: Card 1: cut the letter A. Choose the fold, then Draw, Cut and Open. Which fold do you use and how much of the A do you draw? Answer: the vertical fold, and half (1/2) of the A. The opened cutout is the full A.

Card 2: cut the letter H. Which fold do you use and how much of the H do you draw? Answer: fold both ways into one-fourth, once vertically and once horizontally, and draw a quarter (1/4) of the H. The opened cutout is the full H.

Card 3 (practice values): cut the letter M. Try the Horizontal fold first, then the Vertical fold. Answer: the Horizontal fold gives a cutout that is not an M, because the top and bottom of the M do not match. The Vertical fold gives the full M, with half (1/2) drawn.
Card 4 (practice values): cut the letter B. Which fold works? Answer: the Horizontal fold, with half (1/2) of the B drawn, because the top half and the bottom half of the B match.
Card 5 (practice values): try to cut the letter F with every fold. Answer: no fold gives an F, because the F has no line of symmetry. Its halves never match.

Challenge: 'Which of the following alphabet cutouts can be made by just drawing half (1/2) or quarter (1/4) of the letter? You can do it by drawing lines of symmetry on the letters. E N X T K V O' Cut each letter with the folds. Answer: E, X, T, K, V and O can be cut out, with 1/2 drawn for E, T, K and V and 1/4 drawn for X and O. N cannot, because it has no line of symmetry.

Challenge: 'Which of the letters have a horizontal line of symmetry? Which of the letters have a vertical line of symmetry? Which letters have both vertical and horizontal lines of symmetry?' Use your results sheet. Answer: horizontal line: E, X, K, O. Vertical line: X, T, V, O. Both: X, O.
feedback: After Open, a full letter shows a soft green message such as: The halves matched, so the cutout is the full A. A cutout that is not the letter shows a soft amber message such as: The two halves do not match, so this fold is not a line of symmetry. Try the other fold.
After Draw, the tool says how much of the letter is drawn, for example: You drew 1/2 of the letter. For the two-fold choice it says: You drew 1/4 of the letter.
A tick on the results sheet that does not agree with the cutouts slides back with a clue such as: Cut the letter with the Horizontal fold. Do the halves match?
On the card with the F, after every fold has been tried, the tool says: None of the folds gave an F, so the F has no line of symmetry.
tool_config.done_when: Every practice card is cut with a correct fold, the results sheet is ticked for the letters E, N, X, T, K, V and O, and the student has answered both of the story's questions from the sheet.

hint_ladder.text: Look at the letter. If you folded it, would the two halves land exactly on each other?
Try the Vertical fold, then the Horizontal fold. After each one, look at the opened cutout and ask: is it the full letter?
For this letter, check one side against the other: which fold makes the two halves match?
Use the fold the tool shows, and draw only the part it outlines along the fold. The opened paper shows the full letter.

concepts.concept_name: Fold on a Line of Symmetry

content.text:
The letter A has a vertical line of symmetry. So, to cut out the letter A: 1. Fold a paper in half. 2. Draw half of the letter A along the fold. 3. Cut along the outline. 4. Open the paper to see the full letter A.
The letter H has two lines of symmetry. 1. Fold the paper into one-fourth (once vertically, once horizontally). 2. Draw one-fourth of the letter H along the fold. 3. Cut along the outline. 4. Open the paper to see the full letter H.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Prem folds a paper in half, draws half of the letter A along the fold and cuts along the outline. What will the opened paper show?
2. It shows the full letter A. The letter A has a vertical line of symmetry: the two halves on either side of the line match.
3. A line of symmetry is a line that splits a shape into two halves that match exactly when the shape is folded along it.
4. To cut out the letter A: fold a paper in half, draw half of the letter A along the fold, cut along the outline, and open the paper to see the full letter A.
5. The letter H has two lines of symmetry, one vertical and one horizontal. So fold the paper into one-fourth, once vertically and once horizontally, and draw one-fourth of the letter H along the folds. Cut and open: the full letter H appears.
6. Rule: with one line of symmetry, half (1/2) of the letter is enough. With two lines of symmetry, a quarter (1/4) is enough.

content.text:
Worked example: Prem wants to cut out the letter M from a folded paper. Which fold should Prem use, and how much of the M must be drawn?
1. Look at the M. The left side and the right side match, so the M has a vertical line of symmetry.
2. Fold the paper in half along the vertical line.
3. Draw half of the M, which is 1/2 of the letter, along the fold.
4. Cut along the outline and open the paper: the full M appears.
5. Check: the top and the bottom of the M do not match, so it has no horizontal line. One fold is all that works, and a quarter is not enough.
Answer: Fold the paper in half along the vertical line and draw 1/2 of the M

concepts.concept_name: Horizontal and Vertical Lines of Symmetry

content.text:
1. Predict first: look at the letter B. Does it have a line of symmetry that goes across, or one that goes up and down?
2. A vertical line goes up and down. A horizontal line goes across, from left to right.
3. The letter B has a horizontal line: the top half and the bottom half match. It has no vertical line, because the left side and the right side do not match.
4. Some letters have both. The letter H has a vertical line and a horizontal line.
5. To find a line, imagine folding the letter along a vertical line, then along a horizontal line. If the two halves land exactly on each other, that line is a line of symmetry.
6. Rule: check the vertical line, then the horizontal line, then say vertical, horizontal, both or none.

content.text:
Worked example: Which lines of symmetry do the letters B, W and H have?
1. B: fold along a vertical line. The left side is straight and the right side has two bumps, so the halves do not match. Fold along a horizontal line. The top bump lands on the bottom bump, so the halves match. B has a horizontal line only.
2. W: fold along a vertical line. The left half lands on the right half, so they match. Fold along a horizontal line. The top and the bottom do not match. W has a vertical line only.
3. H: fold along a vertical line and the halves match. Fold along a horizontal line and the halves match. H has both lines.

media.description: Concept video: Show that a letter with a line of symmetry can be cut from folded paper by drawing half of it (one line) or a quarter of it (two lines), as in the cutouts of the letters A and H. It works this example: Prem wants to cut out the letter M from a folded paper. Which fold should Prem use, and how much of the M must be drawn?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: Prem folds a paper in half, draws half of the letter A along the fold and cuts along the outline. What will the opened paper show? It shows the full letter A. The letter A has a vertical line of symmetry: the two halves on either side of the line match. A line of symmetry is a line that splits a shape into two halves that match exactly when the shape is folded along it. To cut out the letter A: fold a paper in half, draw half of the letter A along the fold, cut along the outline, and open the paper to see the full letter A. The letter H has two lines of symmetry, one vertical and one horizontal. So fold the paper into one-fourth, once vertically and once horizontally, and draw one-fourth of the letter H along the folds. Cut and open: the full letter H appears. Rule: with one line of symmetry, half (1/2) of the letter is enough. With two lines of symmetry, a quarter (1/4) is enough. 1. Look at the M. The left side and the right side match, so the M has a vertical line of symmetry. 2. Fold the paper in half along the vertical line. 3. Draw half of the M, which is 1/2 of the letter, along the fold. 4. Cut along the outline and open the paper: the full M appears. 5. Check: the top and the bottom of the M do not match, so it has no horizontal line. One fold is all that works, and a quarter is not enough. Answer: Fold the paper in half along the vertical line and draw 1/2 of the M

modules.module_summary: Quarter, half and three-quarter turns, the windmill firki, shapes that look the same after a turn, and telling reflection symmetry from rotational symmetry in letters, digits and numbers.

segments.summary: A full turn is four quarter turns. A shape has rotational symmetry if it looks the same after a 1/4, 1/2 or 3/4 turn. A dot on the shape keeps track of how far it has turned. Every shape looks the same after a full turn, so only the smaller turns count.

source_topic_ids: Let Us Make a Windmill Firki

content.text:
Lali makes firkis for her friends. Follow the steps given below to make your own firki. 1. Take a square paper. 2. Fold the paper in half diagonally to make two triangles. 3. Open and fold it the other way to make two more triangles. 4. Open it again. You will see an 'X' shape on the paper. 5. Use scissors to cut along the four lines of the 'X'. Stop cutting about halfway to the centre. 6. Take one corner of each triangle and fold it gently towards the centre of the paper. Do not press it flat. 7. Fold every other corner towards the centre. 8. Push a pin through the folded corners and the centre of the paper. 9. Push the pin through a stick or straw.
Make sure the pin is not too tight. Check if your windmill spins when the wind is blowing.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a windmill firki has a dot on one blade. You turn the firki a quarter of the way round. Where does the dot go?
2. A full turn takes the dot all the way round, back to the place it started from.
3. A 1/4 turn is a quarter of the way round. A 1/2 turn is half of the way round, so the dot is on the opposite side. A 3/4 turn is three quarters of the way round.
4. Four quarter turns make a full turn, and two quarter turns make a 1/2 turn.
5. Always turn the shape the same way, for example to the right, and use the dot to see how far it has turned.
6. Rule: a 1/4 turn, a 1/2 turn and a 3/4 turn are all smaller than a full turn, and the dot tells you how far the shape has turned.

content.text:
Worked example: A paper pinwheel has 4 blades and a dot on the top blade. Turn it to the right, the same way each time. Where is the dot after a 1/4 turn, a 1/2 turn and a 3/4 turn?
1. A full turn is 4 quarter turns, so each quarter turn moves the dot on by one blade.
2. After a 1/4 turn the dot moves from the top blade to the right blade.
3. After a second quarter turn the dot is on the bottom blade. Two quarter turns make a 1/2 turn, because 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.
4. After a third quarter turn the dot is on the left blade. Three quarter turns make a 3/4 turn.
5. After the fourth quarter turn the dot is back on the top blade, where it started: a full turn.
6. Check: 1/4 turn, right blade; 1/2 turn, bottom blade; 3/4 turn, left blade; full turn, top blade.
Answer: After a 1/4 turn the dot is on the right blade, after a 1/2 turn on the bottom blade, and after a 3/4 turn on the left blade

concepts.concept_name: Rotational Symmetry: Looks the Same After a Turn

content.text:
Observe the letters below. Do they look the same when turned? Dots have been marked on the letters to keep track of the orientation of letters. You may also cut out the letters and fix the centre point of the letter by a nail or use a tracing paper to check if the letter looks the same when turned.
The letter H has rotational symmetry, as it looks the same when rotated by half a turn. A firki has rotational symmetry, as it looks the same when rotated by 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 turn.

The letter H has rotational symmetry, as it looks the same when rotated by half a turn. A firki has rotational symmetry, as it looks the same when rotated by 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 turn.

content.text:
1. Predict first: turn the letter H by a half turn. Does it look the same as before?
2. Yes. After a 1/2 turn the H looks the same. A shape that looks the same after a turn smaller than a full turn has rotational symmetry.
3. Every shape looks the same after a full turn, so a full turn does not count.
4. The firki looks the same after a 1/4, a 1/2 and a 3/4 turn, so it has rotational symmetry. The letter H lies on its side after a 1/4 turn, so it looks the same after a 1/2 turn only.
5. To check, put a dot on the shape, turn it a 1/4, a 1/2 and a 3/4 turn, and each time ask: does it look the same? You can cut out the shape and fix its centre with a nail, or use tracing paper.
6. Rule: a shape has rotational symmetry if it looks the same after at least one of the turns 1/4, 1/2 or 3/4.

content.text:
Worked example: Does the letter Z have rotational symmetry? Does the letter T? Turn each one by 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4.
1. Z: put a dot on the top left of the Z.
2. After a 1/4 turn the Z lies on its side and looks like an N, so it does not look the same.
3. After a 1/2 turn the Z is upside down and looks the same, with the dot now at the bottom right.
4. After a 3/4 turn the Z lies on its other side and looks like an N again, so it does not look the same.
5. The Z looks the same after a 1/2 turn, so it has rotational symmetry, at 1/2 turn.
6. T: after a 1/4 turn the T lies on its side. After a 1/2 turn it is upside down, with the bar at the bottom. After a 3/4 turn it lies on its other side. None of these looks like the T, so the T has no rotational symmetry.
7. Check: every shape looks the same after a full turn, so the full turn does not count.
Answer: The Z has rotational symmetry, at 1/2 turn. The T has no rotational symmetry

steps: Z: put a dot on the top left of the Z.
After a 1/4 turn the Z lies on its side and looks like an N, so it does not look the same.
After a 1/2 turn the Z is upside down and looks the same, with the dot now at the bottom right.
After a 3/4 turn the Z lies on its other side and looks like an N again, so it does not look the same.
The Z looks the same after a 1/2 turn, so it has rotational symmetry, at 1/2 turn.

T: after a 1/4 turn the T lies on its side. After a 1/2 turn it is upside down, with the bar at the bottom. After a 3/4 turn it lies on its other side. None of these looks like the T, so the T has no rotational symmetry.
Check: every shape looks the same after a full turn, so the full turn does not count.
content.answer: The Z has rotational symmetry, at 1/2 turn. The T has no rotational symmetry

media.context: Symmetrical Designs. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Show quarter, half, three-quarter and full turns with a dot on a turning shape, as with the windmill firki. It works this example: A paper pinwheel has 4 blades and a dot on the top blade. Turn it to the right, the same way each time. Where is the dot after a 1/4 turn, a 1/2 turn and a 3/4 turn?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a windmill firki has a dot on one blade. You turn the firki a quarter of the way round. Where does the dot go? A full turn takes the dot all the way round, back to the place it started from. A 1/4 turn is a quarter of the way round. A 1/2 turn is half of the way round, so the dot is on the opposite side. A 3/4 turn is three quarters of the way round. Four quarter turns make a full turn, and two quarter turns make a 1/2 turn. Always turn the shape the same way, for example to the right, and use the dot to see how far it has turned. Rule: a 1/4 turn, a 1/2 turn and a 3/4 turn are all smaller than a full turn, and the dot tells you how far the shape has turned. 1. A full turn is 4 quarter turns, so each quarter turn moves the dot on by one blade. 2. After a 1/4 turn the dot moves from the top blade to the right blade. 3. After a second quarter turn the dot is on the bottom blade. Two quarter turns make a 1/2 turn, because 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2. 4. After a third quarter turn the dot is on the left blade. Three quarter turns make a 3/4 turn. 5. After the fourth quarter turn the dot is back on the top blade, where it started: a full turn. 6. Check: 1/4 turn, right blade; 1/2 turn, bottom blade; 3/4 turn, left blade; full turn, top blade. Answer: After a 1/4 turn the dot is on the right blade, after a 1/2 turn on the bottom blade, and after a 3/4 turn on the left blade

media.description: Concept video: Explain that a shape has rotational symmetry when it looks the same after a 1/4, 1/2 or 3/4 turn, and that a full turn does not count. It works this example: Does the letter Z have rotational symmetry? Does the letter T? Turn each one by 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: turn the letter H by a half turn. Does it look the same as before? Yes. After a 1/2 turn the H looks the same. A shape that looks the same after a turn smaller than a full turn has rotational symmetry. Every shape looks the same after a full turn, so a full turn does not count. The firki looks the same after a 1/4, a 1/2 and a 3/4 turn, so it has rotational symmetry. The letter H lies on its side after a 1/4 turn, so it looks the same after a 1/2 turn only. To check, put a dot on the shape, turn it a 1/4, a 1/2 and a 3/4 turn, and each time ask: does it look the same? You can cut out the shape and fix its centre with a nail, or use tracing paper. Rule: a shape has rotational symmetry if it looks the same after at least one of the turns 1/4, 1/2 or 3/4. 1. Z: put a dot on the top left of the Z. 2. After a 1/4 turn the Z lies on its side and looks like an N, so it does not look the same. 3. After a 1/2 turn the Z is upside down and looks the same, with the dot now at the bottom right. 4. After a 3/4 turn the Z lies on its other side and looks like an N again, so it does not look the same. 5. The Z looks the same after a 1/2 turn, so it has rotational symmetry, at 1/2 turn. 6. T: after a 1/4 turn the T lies on its side. After a 1/2 turn it is upside down, with the bar at the bottom. After a 3/4 turn it lies on its other side. None of these looks like the T, so the T has no rotational symmetry. 7. Check: every shape looks the same after a full turn, so the full turn does not count. Answer: The Z has rotational symmetry, at 1/2 turn. The T has no rotational symmetry

Check: only a turn smaller than a full turn counts, so the Y has no rotational symmetry.

concepts.concept_name: Reflection Only, Turn Only or Both

content.text:
1. Predict first: the letter M has a vertical line of symmetry. Does it also look the same after a half turn?
2. A shape can have reflection symmetry, rotational symmetry, both, or neither. They are two different tests.
3. Test 1, reflection: fold the shape along a vertical or a horizontal line. Do the halves match?
4. Test 2, rotation: turn the shape a 1/4, a 1/2 and a 3/4 turn. Does it look the same after any of them?
5. M passes Test 1, because it has a vertical line. It does not pass Test 2, because after a 1/2 turn it looks like a W. So M has reflection symmetry only.
6. H passes both tests, so H has both symmetries.
7. Rule: run both tests every time. A line of symmetry does not tell you about turns, and a turn does not tell you about lines.

content.text:
Worked example: Sort the letter M, the letter S and the plus sign into: reflection symmetry only, rotational symmetry only, both symmetries, or neither.
1. M, Test 1: it has a vertical line of symmetry. Test 2: after a 1/2 turn it looks like a W, so it does not look the same. M has reflection symmetry only.
2. S, Test 1: fold it along a vertical line or a horizontal line and the halves do not match, so there is no line of symmetry. Test 2: after a 1/2 turn the S looks the same. S has rotational symmetry only.
3. The plus sign, Test 1: it has a vertical line and a horizontal line. Test 2: it looks the same after a 1/4 turn. It has both symmetries.
4. Check: each of the three signs went to a different group.
Answer: M: reflection symmetry only. S: rotational symmetry only. The plus sign: both

tool_config.idea: Test a letter, a digit or a number with a fold line and with a turn, and sort it into reflection only, turn only, both, or neither, so that the student sees that the two tests give two different answers and runs both every time.
tool_config.screen: Lali's craft table, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A wooden test board in the middle holds one large card at a time, the largest thing on screen, with a letter, a digit or a number on it. Beside the board are two testers. The fold tester has two switches, Fold on the vertical line and Fold on the horizontal line, which draw a dashed line on the card and slide one half over the other so the student sees whether the halves match. The turn tester is a turn dial with three stops, 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4, which turns the card to the right and keeps a dashed outline of the starting position. Under the board four trays stand in a row: Reflection only, Turn only, Both and Neither. A shelf above holds the cards still to be tested. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: tap a card to bring it to the board; tap a fold switch; tap a stop on the dial; drag the card into a tray; Check, Hint, Retry (returns the card to the board), Reset (empties the trays), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs under the board: Vertical line: halves match or do not match; Horizontal line: halves match or do not match; 1/4 turn, 1/2 turn, 3/4 turn: looks the same or looks different; and the number of cards in each tray.

It works this example: Sort the letter M, the letter S and the plus sign into: reflection symmetry only, rotational symmetry only, both symmetries, or neither.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: the letter M has a vertical line of symmetry. Does it also look the same after a half turn? A shape can have reflection symmetry, rotational symmetry, both, or neither. They are two different tests. Test 1, reflection: fold the shape along a vertical or a horizontal line. Do the halves match? Test 2, rotation: turn the shape a 1/4, a 1/2 and a 3/4 turn. Does it look the same after any of them? M passes Test 1, because it has a vertical line. It does not pass Test 2, because after a 1/2 turn it looks like a W. So M has reflection symmetry only. H passes both tests, so H has both symmetries. Rule: run both tests every time. A line of symmetry does not tell you about turns, and a turn does not tell you about lines. 1. M, Test 1: it has a vertical line of symmetry. Test 2: after a 1/2 turn it looks like a W, so it does not look the same. M has reflection symmetry only. 2. S, Test 1: fold it along a vertical line or a horizontal line and the halves do not match, so there is no line of symmetry. Test 2: after a 1/2 turn the S looks the same. S has rotational symmetry only. 3. The plus sign, Test 1: it has a vertical line and a horizontal line. Test 2: it looks the same after a 1/4 turn. It has both symmetries. 4. Check: each of the three signs went to a different group. Answer: M: reflection symmetry only. S: rotational symmetry only. The plus sign: both

steps: The digit 1 is drawn as a plain bar, so test the digits as they are drawn in your maths book.
Reflection: fold each digit along a vertical or a horizontal line. 0, 1 and 8 match on both lines, and 3 matches on a horizontal line. 2, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 9 match on no line.
Rotation: turn each digit a 1/2 turn. 0, 1 and 8 look the same. A 1/2 turn turns 6 into 9 and 9 into 6, so 6 and 9 do not look the same by themselves. 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7 do not look the same.
Both: the digits in both lists are 0, 1 and 8.
Check: 3 is in the first list only, and 6 and 9 are in neither list.

content.question: Now, let us look at the following numbers: 11 and 1001. Do these have rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry or both symmetries?
steps: The digit 1 is drawn as a plain bar. Test each number with a fold line and with a 1/2 turn.
11: fold along the vertical line between the two bars and the halves match. Turn it a 1/2 turn: the two bars swap places and the number looks the same.

1001: fold along the vertical line between the two zeros and the halves match. Turn it a 1/2 turn: the first 1 lands at the end, the last 1 lands at the start, and each 0 still looks like a 0, so the number looks the same.
So 11 and 1001 both have reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry.
content.answer: Both numbers have both symmetries, rotational and reflection

concepts.concept_name: A Design That Looks the Same After a Turn

content.text:
1. Predict first: a design has a circle in the middle and one triangle above it. What must you add so that it looks the same after a half turn?
2. A design looks the same after a 1/2 turn when every part has a matching part on the opposite side of the middle. The top triangle needs a matching triangle at the bottom.
3. For a 1/4 turn every part needs a matching part on each of the four sides: top, right, bottom and left.
4. During a full turn, a design with matching parts on all four sides looks the same 4 times: after a 1/4 turn, a 1/2 turn, a 3/4 turn and the full turn.
5. Rule: to make a design look the same after a turn, copy each part to the place where it would land after that turn.

content.text:
Worked example: A design has a circle in the middle and one triangle above it, pointing up. Add triangles so that the design looks the same after a 1/2 turn, and then after a 1/4 turn.
1. After a 1/2 turn the top triangle lands at the bottom, pointing down. Add a triangle below the circle, pointing down.
2. Now the design has 1 + 1 = 2 triangles, and it looks the same after a 1/2 turn.
3. After a 1/4 turn the top triangle lands on the right, pointing right, and the bottom triangle lands on the left, pointing left. Add a triangle on the right and one on the left.
4. Now the design has 2 + 2 = 4 triangles, one on each side of the circle.
5. The design looks the same after a 1/4 turn, a 1/2 turn, a 3/4 turn and a full turn: 4 times in a full turn.
6. Check: after a 1/4 turn each triangle lands on the place of the next triangle.
Answer: Add a triangle below the circle for a 1/2 turn, then a triangle on the left and on the right for a 1/4 turn

concepts.concept_name: Turn Symmetry and Reflection Symmetry in a Design

content.text:
1. Predict first: a square is cut by its two diagonals into 4 triangles. The top and bottom triangles are orange and the left and right triangles are blue. Does it look the same after a 1/2 turn? After a 1/4 turn?
2. Colours count. After a 1/2 turn orange lands on orange and blue lands on blue, so it looks the same. After a 1/4 turn orange lands on blue, so it does not.
3. To find the lines of symmetry of a design, fold it along a line and check that every shape and every colour lands on the same shape and colour.
4. This design has 2 lines of symmetry, the vertical line and the horizontal line. A diagonal is not a line of symmetry here, because it would put orange on blue.
5. A design can have turn symmetry only, reflection symmetry only, both, or neither.
6. Rule: check the shapes and the colours, with a turn for rotational symmetry and with a fold for reflection symmetry.

content.text:
Worked example: A square is cut by its two diagonals into 4 triangles. The top and bottom triangles are orange and the left and right triangles are blue. Does it look the same after a 1/2 turn? After a 1/4 turn? Find its lines of symmetry.
1. Turn it a 1/2 turn: the top triangle lands on the bottom triangle, both orange, and the left triangle lands on the right triangle, both blue. It looks the same.
2. Turn it a 1/4 turn: the top triangle lands on the right triangle, orange on blue. It does not look the same.
3. Fold along the vertical line: the left triangle lands on the right triangle, blue on blue, and the top and bottom triangles each land on themselves. It is a line of symmetry.
4. Fold along the horizontal line: the top triangle lands on the bottom triangle, orange on orange. It is a line of symmetry.
5. Fold along a diagonal: the top triangle lands on the left triangle, orange on blue. It is not a line of symmetry.
6. Check: the design looks the same after a 1/2 turn, not after a 1/4 turn, and it has 2 lines of symmetry.
Answer: It looks the same after a 1/2 turn but not after a 1/4 turn, and it has 2 lines of symmetry: the vertical line and the horizontal line

media.title: Design Studio

tool_config.title: Design Studio
tool_config.idea: Add, change and colour parts of a design so that it looks the same after a 1/2 turn and after a 1/4 turn, and find its lines of symmetry with a fold line, so that the student sees where each part lands after a turn and that colours count.
tool_config.screen: Lali's craft table, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A large round design board with a pin at its centre and four faint guide marks, at the top, right, bottom and left, fills the middle and is the largest thing on screen. A tray beside it holds 6 light blue squares and 6 pink equilateral triangles with the same side as the squares, the pieces of the book's sheet of shapes, and circles for the book's design, and two pots of colour. A turn dial with three stops, 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4, sits in front of the board. A fold line tool offers four lines, vertical, horizontal and the two diagonals. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag a shape from the tray onto the board; tap a placed shape to turn it a quarter; tap a colour pot and then a part to colour it; choose a stop on the dial to show faint ghost copies of the design where each part would land after that turn, with a red outline round any part that has no partner; choose a fold line to show one half folded over the other and whether the shapes and colours match; Undo, Check, Hint, Retry (clears the design of this card), Reset (empties the board), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the number of shapes on the board, the turn chosen, and for each fold line, matches or does not match, with a card number out of 7.
student_does: Look at a circle with one triangle above it (practice values) on the board. Choose the 1/2 turn and tap the place where the triangle lands, then press Next.

Add shapes so that the design looks the same after a 1/2 turn and then after a 1/4 turn, colour a strip of two squares and a square cut by its diagonals, and test each design with the turns and the fold lines.

Do the book's design questions: Making Designs (a) to (d), the two Let Us Think questions and the reflection question, and the squares and triangles questions, with your own designs sorted into three groups.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): a circle with one triangle above it, pointing up. Add a shape so that the design looks the same after a 1/2 turn. Answer: add a triangle below the circle, pointing down. The design then has 2 triangles and no red outlines after the 1/2 turn.

Card 2 (practice values): from the design of card 1, add shapes so that it looks the same after a 1/4 turn. Answer: add a triangle on the left, pointing left, and one on the right, pointing right. The design then has 4 triangles and looks the same after 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 and a full turn, which is 4 times.

Card 3 (practice values): a strip of 2 squares side by side. Colour the left square orange and the right square blue, then test the 1/2 turn. Answer: after a 1/2 turn the orange square lands on the blue square's place, so the design does not look the same. Colour both squares orange and it does. Colours count.

Card 4 (practice values): a square cut by its two diagonals into 4 triangles. Colour the top and bottom triangles orange and the left and right triangles blue. Test the turns and the four fold lines. Answer: it looks the same after a 1/2 turn but not after a 1/4 turn. The vertical and horizontal fold lines match, and the diagonals do not. It has 2 lines of symmetry.

Challenge: Making Designs. The design is a circle in the middle with a triangle above and below it, each with its point touching the circle, a triangle on the left and right, each with its flat side touching the circle, and a second circle at the point of the right triangle. '(a) Does the design have rotational symmetry? Yes/No. (b) Try to change the design by adding some shape(s) so that the new design looks the same after a 1/2 turn. (c) Now try to modify or add more shapes so that the new design looks the same after 1/4 turn. (d) Do the new designs have reflection symmetry? If yes, draw the lines of symmetry.' Answer: (a) No. (b) add a circle at the left tip. (c) make the four arms equal, with a circle at each tip. (d) yes: 2 lines for (b), 4 lines for (c). Your designs may differ.

Challenge: Let Us Think. 'Does this design look the same after 1/2 turn? Does the design look the same after 1/4 turn?' for the square of four smaller squares, green at the top left and bottom right and pink at the other two. 'Colour the square given in the figure using two colours so that the design looks the same after every 1/4 turn. How many times does this shape look the same during a full turn?' Then the squares and triangles: 'Make different symmetrical designs by using these two shapes', the shape of four squares with a triangle at each end of each row, and 'Sort your designs in 3 categories'. feedback: The ghost copies show where each part lands after the chosen turn. A part with no partner gets a red outline and the tool says: After a 1/2 turn this triangle lands here, and nothing is there. Add a copy of it in that place.
When every part has a partner the tool says in green: Every part lands on a matching part, so the design looks the same after this turn.
A fold line shows the two halves folded over each other. If a shape or a colour does not match, the tool marks it and says, for example: Orange lands on blue, so this line is not a line of symmetry.
When a design is finished the tool shows its result for the turns and the lines, and the student sorts it into only rotational symmetry, only reflection symmetry or both.

hint_ladder.text: Look at the design. After the turn, where does each part land? Is there a part there already?
Choose the turn on the dial. A red outline shows the place that has no partner. What is missing there?
Put a copy of the missing part in the place with the red outline. Then turn again and check the next part.
Add the part the tool shows in the red outlined place. Every part now has a partner, so the design looks the same after the turn.

tool_questions: Card 1 (practice values): a circle with one triangle above it, pointing up. Add a shape so that the design looks the same after a 1/2 turn. Answer: add a triangle below the circle, pointing down. The design then has 2 triangles and no red outlines after the 1/2 turn.

Card 2 (practice values): from the design of card 1, add shapes so that it looks the same after a 1/4 turn. Answer: add a triangle on the left, pointing left, and one on the right, pointing right. The design then has 4 triangles and looks the same after 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 and a full turn, which is 4 times.

Card 3 (practice values): a strip of 2 squares side by side. Colour the left square orange and the right square blue, then test the 1/2 turn. Answer: after a 1/2 turn the orange square lands on the blue square's place, so the design does not look the same. Colour both squares orange and it does. Colours count.

Card 4 (practice values): a square cut by its two diagonals into 4 triangles. Colour the top and bottom triangles orange and the left and right triangles blue. Test the turns and the four fold lines. Answer: it looks the same after a 1/2 turn but not after a 1/4 turn. The vertical and horizontal fold lines match, and the diagonals do not. It has 2 lines of symmetry.

media.title: A Design That Looks the Same After a Turn
media.context: Symmetrical Designs. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Show how to add shapes to a design so that it looks the same after a 1/2 turn and after a 1/4 turn. It works this example: A design has a circle in the middle and one triangle above it, pointing up. Add triangles so that the design looks the same after a 1/2 turn, and then after a 1/4 turn.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a design has a circle in the middle and one triangle above it. What must you add so that it looks the same after a half turn? A design looks the same after a 1/2 turn when every part has a matching part on the opposite side of the middle. The top triangle needs a matching triangle at the bottom. For a 1/4 turn every part needs a matching part on each of the four sides: top, right, bottom and left. During a full turn, a design with matching parts on all four sides looks the same 4 times: after a 1/4 turn, a 1/2 turn, a 3/4 turn and the full turn. Rule: to make a design look the same after a turn, copy each part to the place where it would land after that turn. 1. After a 1/2 turn the top triangle lands at the bottom, pointing down. Add a triangle below the circle, pointing down. 2. Now the design has 1 + 1 = 2 triangles, and it looks the same after a 1/2 turn. 3. After a 1/4 turn the top triangle lands on the right, pointing right, and the bottom triangle lands on the left, pointing left. Add a triangle on the right and one on the left. 4. Now the design has 2 + 2 = 4 triangles, one on each side of the circle. 5. The design looks the same after a 1/4 turn, a 1/2 turn, a 3/4 turn and a full turn: 4 times in a full turn. 6. Check: after a 1/4 turn each triangle lands on the place of the next triangle. Answer: Add a triangle below the circle for a 1/2 turn, then a triangle on the left and on the right for a 1/4 turn

media.title: Turn Symmetry and Reflection Symmetry in a Design
media.context: Symmetrical Designs. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Show how to check shapes and colours for turn symmetry and find the lines of symmetry of a design. It works this example: A square is cut by its two diagonals into 4 triangles. The top and bottom triangles are orange and the left and right triangles are blue. Does it look the same after a 1/2 turn? After a 1/4 turn? Find its lines of symmetry.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a square is cut by its two diagonals into 4 triangles. The top and bottom triangles are orange and the left and right triangles are blue. Does it look the same after a 1/2 turn? After a 1/4 turn? Colours count. After a 1/2 turn orange lands on orange and blue lands on blue, so it looks the same. After a 1/4 turn orange lands on blue, so it does not. To find the lines of symmetry of a design, fold it along a line and check that every shape and every colour lands on the same shape and colour. This design has 2 lines of symmetry, the vertical line and the horizontal line. A diagonal is not a line of symmetry here, because it would put orange on blue. A design can have turn symmetry only, reflection symmetry only, both, or neither. Rule: check the shapes and the colours, with a turn for rotational symmetry and with a fold for reflection symmetry. 1. Turn it a 1/2 turn: the top triangle lands on the bottom triangle, both orange, and the left triangle lands on the right triangle, both blue. It looks the same. 2. Turn it a 1/4 turn: the top triangle lands on the right triangle, orange on blue. It does not look the same. 3. Fold along the vertical line: the left triangle lands on the right triangle, blue on blue, and the top and bottom triangles each land on themselves. It is a line of symmetry. 4. Fold along the horizontal line: the top triangle lands on the bottom triangle, orange on orange. It is a line of symmetry. 5. Fold along a diagonal: the top triangle lands on the left triangle, orange on blue. It is not a line of symmetry. 6. Check: the design looks the same after a 1/2 turn, not after a 1/4 turn, and it has 2 lines of symmetry. Answer: It looks the same after a 1/2 turn but not after a 1/4 turn, and it has 2 lines of symmetry: the vertical line and the horizontal line

steps: (a): look at the right side. There is a circle at the tip of the right triangle, but nothing at the tip of the left triangle. After a 1/2 turn the circle would land on the left, where there is no circle. So the answer is No.

(b): add a circle at the tip of the left triangle. After a 1/2 turn the top triangle lands on the bottom triangle, the left arm lands on the right arm, and the two circles swap. The new design looks the same after a 1/2 turn.

(c): make all four arms the same. Turn the top and bottom triangles round so that their flat sides touch the middle circle, and put a circle at the tip of each of the four triangles. Every arm is now a triangle with a circle at its tip, so the design looks the same after every 1/4 turn.

(d): the design from (b) has 2 lines of symmetry, a vertical line and a horizontal line through the middle circle. The design from (c) has 4 lines: the vertical line, the horizontal line and the two diagonals.

content.answer: (a): No. (b): add a circle at the left tip. (c): four equal arms with a circle at each tip. (d): yes, 2 lines for (b) and 4 lines for (c). Your drawings may differ.

After a 1/4 turn the top left square, green, lands where the top right square is, and that square is pink. The design does not look the same.
Check: the colours decide the answer, so a 1/2 turn works and a 1/4 turn does not.

steps: The dashed lines cut the square into 8 equal triangles round the middle.
A 1/4 turn moves every triangle on by 2 places.
So colour the triangles one after the other in two colours, orange, blue, orange, blue, and so on all the way round.
Now each triangle lands on a triangle of its own colour after a 1/4 turn.
The design looks the same after a 1/4 turn, a 1/2 turn, a 3/4 turn and the full turn: 4 times in a full turn.
Check: 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so 4 quarter turns make a full turn.
content.answer: Colour the 8 triangles in two colours, one after the other. The shape looks the same 4 times in a full turn.

content.book_number: Let Us Think: reflection symmetry in the designs
content.question: Do these designs have reflection symmetry also? Draw the lines of symmetry.
steps: The two designs are the green and pink square and the square coloured orange and blue.
Green and pink square: fold it along a diagonal, from one corner to the opposite corner. The two halves land on each other, green on green and pink on pink. So each diagonal is a line of symmetry.
Fold it along the vertical line: the green square would land on a pink square. That is not a line of symmetry. The horizontal line does the same.
So the green and pink square has 2 lines of symmetry, the two diagonals.
Orange and blue square: fold it along any dashed line. Every triangle would land on a triangle of the other colour. So there is no line of symmetry.
This design looks the same after a turn, but it has no reflection symmetry.
content.answer: Green and pink square: yes, 2 lines (the two diagonals). Orange and blue square: no line of symmetry.

content.question: Cut out squares and equilateral triangles with the same side length. These are provided at the end of the book. Make different symmetrical designs by using these two shapes.
steps: Take squares and equilateral triangles with the same side length.
Place a square in the middle and a triangle on each of its 4 sides, with a side of the triangle along a side of the square. The design looks the same after every 1/4 turn and has 4 lines of symmetry.
Place one triangle on top of one square: a house shape. It has 1 vertical line of symmetry and no turn that makes it look the same.
Place 4 triangles in a row, one pointing up, then one pointing down, and so on. This slanted strip looks the same after a 1/2 turn and has no line of symmetry.
Sample answer: many other designs work. Your answer may differ.
content.answer: Sample answer: a square with a triangle on each side, a house shape, a slanted strip of 4 triangles. Your designs may differ.

[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution]
3. Place one triangle on top of one square: a house shape. It has $1$ vertical line of symmetry and no turn that makes it look the same.
4. Place $4$ triangles in a row, one pointing up, then one pointing down, and so on. This slanted strip looks the same after a $\frac{1}{2}$ turn and has no line of symmetry.
5. Sample answer: many other designs work. Your answer may differ.
Answer: Sample answer: a square with a triangle on each side, a house shape, a slanted strip of $4$ triangles. Your designs may differ.

steps: The shape has 4 squares in 2 rows of 2, and 4 triangles: one at the left end and one at the right end of each row.

Horizontal line: fold along the line between the two rows. The top row lands on the bottom row. It is a second line of symmetry.
Turn: after a 1/4 turn the triangles would land above and below the squares, where there are none, so it does not look the same.
After a 1/2 turn each triangle lands on the triangle at the other end and each square lands on the square opposite to it, so it looks the same. It has rotational symmetry at 1/2 turn.
So the shape has both symmetries.

content.text: Block printing is a traditional craft of Rajasthan, known for beautiful patterns and bright colours. Artisans use carved wooden blocks to print designs on fabric. This art has been practised for centuries and makes Rajasthan's textiles special.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a wooden block has a design carved on it. The print on the cloth shows only half of the design, cut by a straight edge. Where is the other half?
2. Block printing is a traditional craft of Rajasthan, known for beautiful patterns and bright colours. Artisans use carved wooden blocks to print designs on fabric.
3. Many blocks have a line of symmetry. A half print has one straight edge, and that edge is the line of symmetry.
4. The other half is the same picture on the other side of the line, as if the print were folded along it.
5. To match a block to a half print, find the block's line of symmetry, imagine cutting the block along it, and look for the half print with the same shapes along its straight edge.
6. Rule: the two halves of a symmetrical print are the same shape on the two sides of the line of symmetry.

Block printing is a traditional craft of Rajasthan, known for beautiful patterns and bright colours. Artisans use carved wooden blocks to print designs on fabric.
Many blocks have a line of symmetry. A half print has one straight edge, and that edge is the line of symmetry.
The other half is the same picture on the other side of the line, as if the print were folded along it.
To match a block to a half print, find the block's line of symmetry, imagine cutting the block along it, and look for the half print with the same shapes along its straight edge.
Rule: the two halves of a symmetrical print are the same shape on the two sides of the line of symmetry.

content.text:
Worked example: A block is carved in the shape of a leaf with a stem down the middle. Its half print shows only the left half of the leaf. What does the whole print look like?
1. The half print has one straight edge. That edge is the line of symmetry.
2. The straight edge runs down the middle of the leaf, along the stem.
3. Draw the same half on the other side of the line, as if the paper were folded along the edge.
4. The two halves together make the whole leaf.
5. Check: fold the whole print along the line and the two halves land on each other.
Answer: The whole print is the half print together with its copy on the other side of the straight edge

content.text:
Worked example: A flower block is stamped 2 times, with a 1/2 turn between the stamps. Does the print look the same after a 1/2 turn? After a 1/4 turn?
1. The first stamp puts a flower at the top.
2. A 1/2 turn of the block puts the second flower at the bottom.
3. Turn the print a 1/2 turn: the top flower lands at the bottom and the bottom flower lands at the top. The print looks the same.
4. Turn the print a 1/4 turn: the flowers would land at the sides, where there are none. The print does not look the same.
5. Check: 2 stamps match after a 1/2 turn only.
Answer: After a 1/2 turn it looks the same, and after a 1/4 turn it does not

media.title: A Half Print and Its Line of Symmetry
media.context: Symmetrical Designs. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Show that the straight edge of a half print is the line of symmetry, so a half print and its copy make the whole print, and how to match a block to its half print. It works this example: A block is carved in the shape of a leaf with a stem down the middle. Its half print shows only the left half of the leaf. What does the whole print look like?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a wooden block has a design carved on it. The print on the cloth shows only half of the design, cut by a straight edge. Where is the other half? Block printing is a traditional craft of Rajasthan, known for beautiful patterns and bright colours. Artisans use carved wooden blocks to print designs on fabric. Many blocks have a line of symmetry. A half print has one straight edge, and that edge is the line of symmetry. The other half is the same picture on the other side of the line, as if the print were folded along it. To match a block to a half print, find the block's line of symmetry, imagine cutting the block along it, and look for the half print with the same shapes along its straight edge. Rule: the two halves of a symmetrical print are the same shape on the two sides of the line of symmetry. 1. The half print has one straight edge. That edge is the line of symmetry. 2. The straight edge runs down the middle of the leaf, along the stem. 3. Draw the same half on the other side of the line, as if the paper were folded along the edge. 4. The two halves together make the whole leaf. 5. Check: fold the whole print along the line and the two halves land on each other. Answer: The whole print is the half print together with its copy on the other side of the straight edge

content.book_number: Block Printing: design B
content.question: The design B looks the same after every ___ turn. This design has ___ symmetry.
steps: The design B is made of 4 hearts placed round the middle.
Turn it a 1/4 turn: the top heart lands where the right heart is, the right heart where the bottom heart is, and so on. The design looks the same after every 1/4 turn.
The dashed vertical line and the dashed horizontal line are lines of symmetry: the left half matches the right half, and the top half matches the bottom half.
So the design has rotational symmetry and reflection symmetry.
Check: it looks the same after a turn and it has lines of symmetry, so it has both.
content.answer: Every 1/4 turn. It has both rotational symmetry and reflection symmetry.
content.text:

2. Turn it a $\frac{1}{4}$ turn: the top heart lands where the right heart is, the right heart where the bottom heart is, and so on. The design looks the same after every $\frac{1}{4}$ turn.

steps: Test each shape with a fold line (reflection symmetry) and with a turn (rotational symmetry). The shapes are numbered 1 to 19 round the border from the top-left corner, going to the right, then down, then to the left, then up.

Shape 2, the green six-pointed star: 6 lines, and it looks the same after a 1/6 turn. Tick and star.
Shape 3, the yellow six-sided shape: it has a vertical line and a horizontal line of symmetry, and it looks the same after a 1/2 turn. Tick and star.
Shape 4, three lilac circles joined to the middle, drawn nearly even: 3 lines, and a 1/3 turn. Tick and star.
Shape 5, the green triangle with grey corners: 3 lines, and a 1/3 turn. Tick and star.
Shape 6, the pink rectangle: 2 lines, and a 1/2 turn. Tick and star.

Shape 12, the pink triangle with three teal circles: 3 lines, and a 1/3 turn. Tick and star.
Shape 13, the orange slanted four-sided shape: no line of symmetry, but it looks the same after a 1/2 turn. Star only.
Shape 14, the yellow triangle with three small grey triangles: 3 lines, and a 1/3 turn. Tick and star.
Shape 15, the thin pink triangle with a square corner: no line of symmetry and no turn that works. No mark.
Shape 16, the two maroon triangles touching at their points: 2 lines, and a 1/2 turn. Tick and star.
Shape 17, the circle: every line through the middle is a line of symmetry, and it looks the same after every turn. Tick and star.

content.book_number: Project Work: vegetable blocks
content.question: Create symmetrical patterns and designs using vegetable blocks. Some are shown below.
steps: Cut a vegetable, such as a potato, to get a flat face, and carve a simple shape on it. A ladyfinger cut across also gives a flower-like face.
Dip the flat face in colour and press it on paper to make a print.
For a design that looks the same after every 1/4 turn, stamp the block, turn the paper a 1/4 turn, and stamp again, 4 times in all.
For a design with a line of symmetry, use a block that has its own line of symmetry and stamp it on the two sides of a line drawn on the paper, the same distance from the line.
Sort your prints: only rotational symmetry, only reflection symmetry, or both.
Sample answer: your patterns may be different. Your answer may differ.
content.answer: Sample answer: print a vegetable block 4 times, turning a 1/4 turn each time, and sort your prints. Your answer may differ.

content.text:
1. Predict first: you have walked round the whole craft table. Can you say one idea from each stop, from the folded paper to the block prints? Read the lines below and tick each idea you remembered.
2. Line of symmetry: a line that splits a shape into two halves that match when the shape is folded along it. A letter with one line of symmetry can be cut out of folded paper by drawing 1/2 of it, and a letter with two lines by drawing 1/4 of it.
3. Check: the letter A has a vertical line, so draw 1/2 of the A along the fold. The letter H has two lines, so draw 1/4 of the H.
4. A horizontal line goes across and a vertical line goes up and down. A letter can have a horizontal line, a vertical line, both or none.
5. Turns: a full turn is four quarter turns, and 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 1. Two quarter turns make a 1/2 turn.
6. Rotational symmetry: a shape looks the same after a 1/4, 1/2 or 3/4 turn. The firki does. The letter H does after a 1/2 turn. The letter Y does not.
7. Check: does the letter Z look the same after a 1/2 turn? Yes. After a 1/4 turn? No.
8. Two tests: fold for reflection symmetry and turn for rotational symmetry. M has reflection symmetry only, S has rotational symmetry only, and the plus sign has both.
9. Digits: 0, 1 and 8 have both symmetries. 3 has reflection symmetry only. 6 and 9 turn into each other, so neither looks the same after a 1/2 turn by itself.
10. Designs: to make a design look the same after a 1/2 turn, give every part a matching part on the opposite side. For a 1/4 turn, give every part a matching part on all four sides. Colours count too.
11. Check: a square of 4 smaller squares, green at the top left and bottom right and pink at the other two, looks the same after a 1/2 turn but not after a 1/4 turn.
12. Block prints: the straight edge of a half print is the line of symmetry. A block stamped 4 times, a 1/4 turn each time, makes a print that looks the same after every 1/4 turn.
13. Check: a flower block stamped 2 times with a 1/2 turn between looks the same after a 1/2 turn.

objectives.objective_text: Students fold a paper along a line of symmetry and draw half or a quarter of a letter along the fold to make the full letter cutout.
Students name the horizontal and the vertical lines of symmetry of a letter and say which letters have both lines.
Students find which letters can be cut out by drawing half or a quarter, and name the letters with a horizontal line, a vertical line or both lines of symmetry.
Students describe a 1/4 turn, a 1/2 turn, a 3/4 turn and a full turn, and say where a dot on a turning shape lands after each turn.
Students turn a shape by 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4 and decide whether it has rotational symmetry by checking if it looks the same after a turn.
Students say whether the firki and the letters H, I, X and Y look the same after 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 and a full turn, and name the turn of their rotational symmetry.
Students use a fold test and a turn test to decide whether a letter or sign has reflection symmetry only, rotational symmetry only, both or neither.
Students find the digits and numbers with reflection symmetry, rotational symmetry or both, and give examples of 2-, 3- and 4-digit numbers of each kind.
Students add shapes to a design so that it looks the same after a 1/2 turn and after a 1/4 turn, and count the turns at which the design matches in a full turn.
Students check shapes and colours to find whether a design looks the same after a turn, and find its lines of symmetry by folding.
Students change and colour designs so that they look the same after a 1/2 turn and a 1/4 turn, and draw the lines of symmetry of the designs.
Students match a wooden block to its half print by finding the line of symmetry along the straight edge of the print.
Students explain why a block stamped 2 times with a 1/2 turn, or 4 times with 1/4 turns, makes a print that looks the same after that turn.
Students match blocks to their half prints, name the turn and the symmetry of a block print, mark border shapes for reflection and rotational symmetry, and plan a vegetable-block project.

Book item: Look at the letters E, N, X, T, K, V and O. (a): Which of the letters have a horizontal line of symmetry? ___; (b): Which of the letters have a vertical line of symmetry? ___; (c): Which letters have both vertical and horizontal lines of symmetry? ___

Book item: Observe the dot in the firki. Does the firki look the same after 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, and a full turn? ___

Book item: Observe the letter H. Dots have been marked on it to keep track of its orientation. Does the H look the same after a 1/4 turn, a 1/2 turn, a 3/4 turn and a full turn? Does it have rotational symmetry? Yes/No.

Book item: Observe the letters. Dots have been marked on the letters to keep track of the orientation of letters. You may also cut out the letters and fix the centre point of the letter by a nail or use a tracing paper to check if the letter looks the same when turned. Does it have rotational symmetry (Yes/No)?

Book item: Find symmetry in the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 0. (a): Which digit(s) have reflection symmetry? ___; (b): Which digit(s) have rotational symmetry? ___; (c): Which digit(s) have both rotational and reflection symmetries? ___
Book item: Now, let us look at the following numbers: 11 and 1001. Do these have (a): rotational symmetry, (b): reflection symmetry or (c) both symmetries?
Book item: Give examples of 2-, 3-, and 4-digit numbers which have rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry, or both.

Book item: (a): Does the design have rotational symmetry? Yes/No. (b): Try to change the design by adding some shape(s) so that the new design looks the same after a 1/2 turn. Book item: Do these designs have reflection symmetry also? Draw the line(s) of symmetry.
Book item: Cut out squares and equilateral triangles with the same side length. These are provided at the end of the book. Make different symmetrical designs by using these two shapes.
Book item: Does this shape have reflection symmetry? If yes, draw its line(s) of symmetry. Does it have rotational symmetry? If yes, at which turn? Does it have both symmetries?

Book item: Now, make your designs. Sort your designs in 3 categories: designs with only rotational symmetry, designs with only reflection symmetry, and designs with both rotational and reflection symmetry.
